newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says settlement halt condition for summit.
newsitem.headline: PLO says settlement halt condition for summit.

text.p: The PLO said on Friday Israel had to stop building a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem before Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would agree to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
His response came only a few hours after the Israeli premier offered to meet U.S. and Palestinian leaders for three-way Camp David-style talks if necessary to forge a final Middle East peace deal.

"They (the Israelis) have to stop building the settlement in East Jerusalem and the Americans have to guarantee Israel is committed to the signed agreements," Arafat's spokesman Nabil Abu Rdeineh said when questioned about Netanyahu's proposal.
Netanyahu, facing a crisis in the peace process and clashes in the West Bank, told Germany's ARD television he was ready to meet the other two leaders for peace talks.

He has repeatedly rejected appeals by the Palestinians, the Arab world and the international community to halt work on the Har Homa settlement in Arab East Jerusalam that has sparked 16 days of West Bank rage and Israeli-Palestinian clashes.

Israel and the Palestinians both claim East Jerusalem as their own. Palestinians fear Israel's construction in the part of the city it captured from Jordan in 1967 strengthens its hand in future talks on the city's final status.

"As soon as violence against us stops, we can clear up all outstanding questions in six months," Netanyahu said in the interview ahead of a crisis meeting with President Bill Clinton at the White House on Monday.

"If we don't manage that within that time, then Arafat, President Clinton and I can try to settle the Israeli- Palestinian dispute in a sort of Camp David summit," he said, referring to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

In 1978 13 days of intensive U.S.-Israeli-Egyptian talks at the U.S. presidential retreat in Camp David near Washington paved the way for Israel's peace treaty with Egypt, its first with an Arab state, a year later.
Abu Rdeineh doubted conditions were ripe for a similar diplomatic marathon.
"The Palestinian leadership is studying all the proposals," he told Reuters, but added: "We are still waiting for the American initiative to push the peace process forward."

Palestinian negotiator Hassan Asfour balked at Netanyahu's offer to skip over an existing deal on phased Israeli West Bank troop pullbacks and instead race to complete "final status" peace talks within half a year. "This is a black joke," he said.

Washington, the main sponsor of interim peace deals signed by Israel and the Palestinians since 1993, has so far described as premature reports in the U.S. and Israeli news media of a possible Camp David summit to clinch an Israeli-PLO deal.
"We haven't decided on anything yet. We're at the sifting-through stage," one U.S. official said this week.

Under the existing deal, Israel is due to withdraw from West Bank rural areas in three phases by mid-1998 and to seal a final peace deal with the PLO by May 1999. The PLO wants to receive more territory before closing a final accord.

Palestinians have not ruled out a Camp David-style summit but doubt Washington's ability to be an honest broker after it twice vetoed U.N. Security Council resolutions to censure Israel over the Jerusalem settlement.

While talks have stalled, Israeli troops have shot dead three Palestinians in the unrest. A suicide bomber killed three Israelis in a Tel Aviv blast. Two Palestinians died in botched suicide attacks in Gaza.
